title: The Qualities of a Great Teammate
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article portrays being a great teammate as a compounding career asset, since trusted colleagues are given more information, more input into decisions, and more candid peer feedback than others. It walks through familiar qualities like dependability, emotional stability, and accountability before turning to less obvious ones, including sharing credit freely and fully committing to decisions even after voicing disagreement beforehand. Its central claim is that the best teammates go further still, coaching and holding others to team standards without any formal authority to do so. The piece closes by framing every quality described as an informal act of leadership, which is why great teammates tend to eventually earn the title of leader.
points: Being a great teammate is framed as a compounding career asset that earns advocacy from others over time.
Trusted teammates receive more information, more input into decisions, and more candid peer feedback.
Beyond dependability and emotional stability, great teammates share credit freely and fully commit to decisions after voicing dissent beforehand.
Exceptional teammates coach and hold others to team standards without any formal authority to do so.
The article frames every described quality as leadership practiced without permission, which is why titles eventually catch up to great teammates.
quotes: Being the teammate everyone wants to work with is a career asset that appreciates over time.
Because the best learning in organizations comes from peers, not training programs, great teammates receive more insights, best practices, and candid feedback.
They understand the difference between voicing dissent before a decision is made and undermining it afterward.
Every quality described here, from dependability to full commitment, is really a form of leadership practiced without permission or authority.
Great teammates are those leaders. The title eventually catches up to them.
